issues.issue: The Agreement is said to consist of Parts I-VI plus Rate Sheets and Fee Schedules "published by the Bank from time to time," so its content is not fixed at contracting.
This provision makes Part VI (Night Depository) part of a single Agreement, while the Night Depository "Entire Agreement" clause states that it constitutes the entire agreement as to that service.

"Account" is defined subject to the open-ended qualifier "as applicable, unless limited by the heading under which it appears," so the scope of the defined term shifts with each heading and cannot be fixed.
The definition omits Health Savings Accounts, Holiday Club and Club Saver Accounts, which the Right of Set-Off clause and the Withdrawal Policy nonetheless treat as Accounts.
"You" is limited to depositors and joint owners, yet the Trust Account and UTMA provisions address "you as trustee" and "you, as custodian," and Part VI defines "you" as the Depositor.
The clause claims that any variance from the UCC is controlled by the Agreement, without identifying which provisions vary or acknowledging the UCC terms that cannot be varied by agreement.
"Additional reasonable charges" is not defined and no benchmark is supplied for measuring reasonableness.

The clause imposes charges for services "not contemplated by this Agreement but ... disclosed in our Personal Fee Schedule," though the introduction makes the Personal Fee Schedule part of the Agreement.
The final sentence refers to "a charge or transaction described in this disclosure," but no charge is described anywhere in this provision or Part I.
Consent is given for "any telephone or cell phone calls placed to you by us or our agents" with no limit on purpose or duration, leaving open whether collection or marketing calls are covered.

The clause declares the parties' survivorship intent as a matter of form ("Each of you intends") from the mere act of signing a signature card, which invites a dispute over whether that recital reflects the depositor's actual intent.

The provision states that "None of you may instruct us to take away any of the rights of another," yet the same paragraph lets any one owner stop payment on joint deposits and force written authorization from all owners.
"Authorized Signer" is capitalized as if a defined term but is never defined anywhere in the Agreement.

It limits changes and withdrawals for "either of these Trust Account types" to what the trust instrument or court order permits, but the Unwritten Trust provision covers accounts with no instrument and lets the trustee withdraw all funds during life.
"We will usually give you provisional credit" and "if we believe in our discretion that your item will not be paid" set no ascertainable standard for when credit is given or withheld.

It states that "The Funds Availability Policy does not apply to items we have accepted for collection only," while the Non-U.S. Financial Institutions section of that Policy fixes availability periods for collection items.
"Typically, the Bank will cash checks" and "adequate available funds" state no enforceable obligation or threshold.
The Bank reserves an unqualified seven-day notice right for Savings and Money Market Accounts, while the parallel sub-account provision states that the Bank "does not presently exercise this right."

The provision says federal regulations "permit ... no more than a combined total of six (6)" such transfers, then provides for a fee "for each such withdrawal in excess of six (6)," so it both forbids and prices the same conduct.

The assertion that transfers back "meet these transactional needs, so there is no adverse impact on the availability of the balances" is a conclusion rather than a term, and sits against an unfettered discretion to set the transfer threshold.
It says the Bank "does not presently exercise" the seven-day notice right, while the Withdrawal Policy reserves the same right for all Savings and Money Market Accounts without that qualification.
Item (f), "there may be other reasons why we may be required to do so under applicable law," is an open catch-all appended to five specific enumerated triggers.

This clause promises a periodic statement for all but listed account types, while Part IV's Periodic Statements clause promises monthly statements only if checks are written or electronic transfers occur, and quarterly otherwise.
The duties are stated only in hortatory and undefined terms — "promptly," "at once," "as soon as possible" — while the following section fixes hard 14- and 30-day limits.
A refusal or failure to cooperate is deemed "ratifi[cation] [of] the defect in the item," a deemed-ratification rule with no stated limit on how minor the failure may be.

The provision fixes fourteen Calendar Days as a "reasonable amount of time" to review and report, then bars claims not reported within thirty Calendar Days, leaving the relationship between the two periods to be construed.

The thirty-day bar on claims about "any error, forgery or other problem" on a statement cannot be squared with Part IV's sixty-Calendar-Day period for reporting unauthorized transfers shown on the same statement.
It treats a Health Savings Account as an Account for statement purposes, though the definition of "Account" in the Definitions section does not include Health Savings Accounts.
"All negotiable paper (called 'checks')" sweeps in instruments that are not checks, and "a form supplied by or previously approved by the Bank" leaves approval standards unstated.

The second sentence begins "But if there is no stop payment order on file ... we may elect to pay it," although the first sentence already gives an unconditional election not to pay; the adversative "But" leaves the two elections in an unclear relation.
"You agree to assume all losses that could have been prevented" states a counterfactual causation test with no standard for judging what safeguarding would have prevented.

The definition ends with the catch-all "any other instruction or order for the payment, transfer or withdrawal of funds" after a long list of specific instruments, leaving the catch-all's reach open to ejusdem generis argument.
"Available Account balance" is the operative measure but is nowhere defined, and the deduction of pending authorizations is qualified by an unspecified "subject to certain exceptions."

This clause makes the balance turn on pending authorizations, while the Overdrafts section defines an overdraft by reference to funds "available in accordance with the Bank's Funds Availability Policy," a different measure.

Category (iii) lumps "all other Account fees" together with "all other items," and the largest-to-smallest rule is stated only "within" categories, leaving the treatment of items straddling categories uncertain.

Overdraft fees are posted in category (ii), ahead of the checks and debit card items in category (iii), yet the following section says overdraft fees are assessed on items that bring the Account negative.

The clause says fees are assessed on items that bring the Account "into a negative balance" but also that pending authorizations "reduce your available balance" without incurring a fee, leaving unclear which balance triggers the fee.
It promises "advance notice" of any change in processing order, while the Amendments clause reserves the right to give only such notice "as we determine is appropriate."
Sub-paragraph (e), "we believe is otherwise not properly payable," is an open catch-all sitting against four specific enumerated grounds for refusal.
"Restrictive legend" is illustrated by two examples "and the like," leaving unclear whether ordinary restrictions such as "For Deposit Only" fall within it.

Debits initiated by a party to whom account information was given are "deemed authorized," while the Unauthorized Transfers section gives the customer rights for transfers "made without your permission using information from your check."

An overdraft is defined by funds available "in accordance with the Bank's Funds Availability Policy," but the next clause and the processing-order clause measure overdrafts by the "negative available balance" after deducting pending authorizations.

The $5 daily allowance and the sentence charging "for each transaction that overdraws your account" once the day-end negative balance exceeds $5 do not say whether the transactions within the first $5 are themselves chargeable.

Fee terms are referred out to an "Important Information for Consumers about your TD Bank Checking Account" brochure, which the introductory clause does not list among the documents comprising the Agreement.
A stop payment request must be received "in such timely manner so as to give the Bank a reasonable opportunity to act" and must "precisely identify" five data points, neither standard being fixed.
"Reasonable time" is said to "depend on the circumstances" and then given a one-way safe harbor, leaving it uncertain whether anything slower can ever be reasonable.
It promises recovery of actual loss "up to the face amount of the check," which cannot be reconciled with the Limited Liability clause capping recovery at three months of fees paid.
New fee rules take effect "after the Change Date" while the parallel interest rules take effect "on the day" of the change, leaving the Change Date itself unassigned for fees.

It requires indemnity for losses from legal action "involving you or your Account," including interpleader the Bank itself commences, while the general Indemnity clause excludes "claims that you may assert against us."

"Upon initiation of an interpleader action, we will be relieved and discharged of all further duties and obligations" does not say whether the discharge is limited to the disputed funds or extends to the whole relationship.
The right arises on "any debt you owe us that is in default," but the Agreement defines default only for an Account, not for a debt, leaving the trigger unfixed.
It allows a hold whenever "we have a claim against you," whereas the Right of Set-Off clause conditions the underlying remedy on a debt that is in default.
The security interest covers "your deposit Accounts" without exception, while the Right of Set-Off clause immediately above excludes IRA, Health Savings and Coverdell Accounts.

The cap is subject to anything "expressly prohibited or otherwise restricted by ... this Agreement," a self-referential carve-out that leaves the cap's own reach uncertain, and liability turns on the undefined phrase "bad faith."

The cap of three months' fees cannot be reconciled with the Stop Payments clause promising recovery up to the face amount of the check or with Part IV's "Our Liability" promise of liability for losses or damages.

The disclaimer of any fiduciary or special relationship sits awkwardly with the Trust Account and fiduciary/custody Account provisions, which contemplate the Bank holding accounts in a fiduciary form.
Default arises if "we, in our sole discretion, are not satisfied with your condition or affairs, financial or otherwise," an open-ended trigger appended to seven specific enumerated events.

The waiver reaches actions arising out of "THE DEALINGS OF THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOU OR US" — a phrase that is both grammatically defective ("OR" for "AND") and of uncertain scope beyond the Account.
"[F]or any reason, or no reason without notice to you" is punctuated so that it is unclear whether "without notice" qualifies both branches or only the second.

Deeming a zero-balance Account "closed by you" after forty-five days does not sit easily with the Abandoned Accounts clause, which contemplates the Bank holding and escheating funds in unused Accounts.
The Account is made subject to "our usual banking practices" and then to "general commercial banking practices in the area we serve," neither of which is defined or ascertainable from the document.

Subjecting the Account to the Bank's own usual practices is hard to square with the Limited Liability section's statement that the Bank's internal policies and procedures "do not impose on us a higher standard of care."
Governing law is tied to "the Store where you opened your Account," which supplies no answer for Accounts opened online, by mail or by telephone.
The Night Depository Agreement instead applies "the state laws that apply to your primary deposit account," a different and undefined connecting factor.
The Bank may change any term "at any time" and give only "such notice of the change as we determine is appropriate," a self-judging notice standard with no fixed content or timing.
It cannot be squared with Part II's Fees & Charges clause, which promises notice "at least thirty (30) days in advance of any changes to these fees."
"Accounts" is redefined for Part II to include ALL personal deposit Accounts, which is broader than the Definitions section's "Account" and creates two operative meanings of the same term.
It conditions the disclosed APY on maintaining the minimum tier balance "each day," while the tier clauses (2A-2E) say the rate for the appropriate tier is paid on the full balance in the Account.

It fixes a rate for "Non-personal TD Relationship Savings accounts," although Part II states that the Accounts covered are ALL personal deposit Accounts and the instrument is a Personal Deposit Account Agreement.
A one-off "Immediate transfer" is made to qualify, although the immediately preceding definition requires a qualifying transfer to be a "recurring transfer."
The clause directs the reader to "The Chart on page 31" while the balance tier structure it describes is set out immediately below it on the same page, a cross-reference error.
The penalty table uses the shorthand "90 days < 1 year" and "1 year < 2 years," leaving the endpoints of each band, and the treatment of a term of exactly one or two years, unstated.
The table expressly applies its penalties to "No Catch" CDs, while the "No Catch" CD clause promises one principal withdrawal during the term with no penalty.
"More than one withdrawal of principal during the term of this CD may result in a penalty" does not say when or what penalty, leaving the customer's exposure indeterminate.

The promise of a penalty-free principal withdrawal conflicts with the Early Withdrawal Penalties table, which lists "No Catch" CDs among the terms carrying interest penalties, and with its rule that no principal may be withdrawn without the Bank's consent.
A single "Immediate transfer" is made to qualify although the definition in the preceding sub-paragraph requires a recurring transfer of at least $25.
The promise of thirty days' advance notice of fee changes conflicts with the Amendments clause, which reserves the right to give only such notice as the Bank determines is appropriate.
This $100-deposit Direct Deposit bonus and the $100-deposit cash bonus in the first paragraph are triggered by the same act, yet each says it "cannot be combined with any other offer."

Eligibility turns on depositing "money not already on deposit at TD Bank" / "new to bank money," a source-tracing test the clause does not explain, and "Maximum deposit limits may apply" states no limit.

The Policy is applied to "all transaction accounts such as Checking and Interest Bearing Checking Accounts, and to Money Market, Savings, and Time Accounts," with "Time Accounts" nowhere defined and "such as" leaving the class open.
The "general policy" of first-Business-Day availability is stated flatly, yet the Longer Delays and Special Rules For New Accounts clauses permit second-, fifth- and seventh-day availability.
"[T]he earliest time that we stop accepting deposits ... for same-day credit is 8pm" states only a floor, not the actual cut-off, and the sentence runs on into "Thus" with no punctuation.
Night depository funds are deemed deposited on the next Business Day the Bank is open, while Part VI's Processing Deposits clause allows two Business Days after receipt of the bag before credit.

Same-day availability of $100 from non-cash teller deposits is hard to reconcile with the Longer Delays clause, which makes "[t]he first $200 of your deposit" available no later than the first Business Day after deposit.

The list of grounds for extended delay includes the open-ended "we believe a check you deposited will not be paid" and "there is an emergency, such as failure of communications or computer equipment," the latter an illustration rather than a defined class.

The new-Customer window is thirty days here, while the immediately following ATM rules apply a ninety-day window and the Same Day Availability clause keys ATM credit to "accounts opened longer than 90 days."
The ninety-day ATM window cannot be squared with the thirty-day new-Customer window stated for the same Special Rules two paragraphs earlier.

It delays ATM cash deposits of new Customers to the first Business Day, while the Same Day Availability clause makes cash deposits available the same day and the ATM deposit timing clause treats a pre-8pm ATM deposit as made that day.

The sentence "funds ... are generally available within thirty (30) Calendar Days or subject to payment by the Drawee bank" is grammatically incoherent, so it is unclear whether thirty days is a limit or merely an estimate.

It sets availability periods for collection items, while the Deposit Policy states that the Funds Availability Policy "does not apply to items we have accepted for collection only" and that no credit is given until final credit is received.

The statement that an authorized purchase cannot be returned unpaid "even if your account is not in good standing" is hard to reconcile with the clause allowing the Bank to refuse any item that would create an overdraft and with "We do not have to allow you to make an overdraft."
"Visa signature transactions and Visa cash advances – $5,000 each" does not say whether the $5,000 is a separate limit for each category or a per-transaction limit.
Termination is provided for "the Electronic Funds Transfer Agreement," a defined-sounding instrument that appears nowhere else; Part IV is styled a disclosure, not an agreement.

The introductory clause states that the Agreement consists of Parts I-VI plus rate and fee schedules, so there is no separable "Electronic Funds Transfer Agreement" that could be terminated on its own.

The applicable rate is "a rate selected by Visa from the range of rates available in wholesale markets," which may vary from the rate Visa itself receives — a description that fixes no ascertainable rate.

The promise of a monthly statement where the only transfers are direct deposits sits against the Periodic Statements clause, which withholds a monthly statement in a month with no checks or electronic transfers.

"[U]nless there are no checks written or no electronic transfers in a particular month" uses "or" where the sense requires "and," so on its face a month with checks but no transfers defeats the monthly statement.

It cannot be squared with Part I's Periodic Statement clause, which promises a periodic statement to every Account other than Holiday Club, Club Saver, IRA, Passbook and CD Accounts without that qualification.
Unlike the Part I Stop Payments clause, this one fixes no duration for a stop order on pre-authorized transfers, leaving it unclear whether the one-year rule carries over.

"[P]urchases made by telephone, on the Internet, or with your Visa Debit Card" does not say whether it captures recurring pre-authorized transfers that happen to have been set up by telephone or online.
It denies any stop payment for such purchases, while the Right to Stop Payment clause immediately above says pre-authorized transfers "can be discontinued" on three Business Days' notice.

The unqualified promise that "we will be liable for your losses or damages" cannot be squared with the Limited Liability clause capping recovery at three months' fees and excluding consequential loss.

The statement that "you may not stop payment of electronic fund transfers" runs against the Right to Stop Payment clause allowing pre-authorized transfers to be discontinued, saved only by the opening words "Unless otherwise provided in the Agreement."
After ten enumerated exceptions the clause adds "There may be other exceptions stated in our Agreement with you," an open-ended catch-all that undoes the closed list.

The opening promise that "we will be liable for losses or damages" cannot be reconciled with the Limited Liability clause, which caps recovery at three months' fees and excludes liability absent bad faith.

The privacy promise is subject to nine exceptions including "certain routine disclosures" and "certain third parties with whom we have joint marketing agreements," categories the clause does not delimit.

The rights it gives for transfers made "without your permission using information from your check" are hard to square with the Pre-authorized Drafts clause, which deems any debit initiated by a party given account information to be authorized.

The sixty-Calendar-Day window for reporting unauthorized transfers shown on a statement conflicts with Part I's thirty-Calendar-Day bar on claims about any error or problem shown on an Account statement.
The sixty-Calendar-Day period for reporting EFT errors sits against Part I's thirty-Calendar-Day bar on claims about errors shown on an Account statement.
"If we decide to do this, we will credit your Account" has an ambiguous antecedent — "this" could refer to taking forty-five days, ninety days, or extending the investigation generally.
The refund entitlement up to the amount of the substitute check plus interest is hard to reconcile with the Limited Liability clause capping recovery at three months of fees paid.
The forty-Calendar-Day claim period runs against Part I's thirty-Calendar-Day bar on asserting any claim about a matter shown on an Account statement.
Part VI uses "this Agreement" to mean the Night Depository Agreement alone, although "Agreement" is defined at the front of the document as the whole instrument including Part VI.
It presents itself as a standalone agreement governing use of the service, while the introductory clause states that the Agreement consists of Parts I-VI together.
"Existing Depositors" is undefined and its boundary against the "new Depositors" of the preceding sub-paragraph is fixed only by the September 1, 2011 date stated there.
The Carrier is deemed to act as "your exclusive agent" while the same clause says the Bank "may arrange for and pay for" that Carrier, leaving the agency characterisation open to attack.

The clause disclaims responsibility for loss "resulting from any cause whatsoever" and then excepts loss "directly caused by our negligence or willful misconduct," leaving the reach of "directly caused" and of "at your own risk" unresolved.

Liability here turns on negligence or willful misconduct, whereas the Part I Limited Liability clause excuses the Bank altogether unless it "HAS ACTED IN BAD FAITH" and caps damages at three months' fees.

Making the employee's determination "conclusive as to the contents of the bags" cannot be squared with the next clause's undertaking to "use ordinary care and adhere to the reasonable commercial standards of the banking business" in processing those contents.

The two-Business-Day counting period conflicts with the Funds Availability Policy that the same sentence says applies, under which night depository deposits are treated as made on the next Business Day.
It refers to "the Deposit Account Agreement" as a separate instrument, although Part VI is itself part of that Agreement under the introductory clause.

An entire-agreement clause covering the night depository service cannot be squared with the introductory clause, which states that the Agreement consists of Parts I-VI together with the Fee Schedules, nor with the conflict-of-terms clause that follows it.

The clause posits a conflict "between any provision of this Agreement and any provision of the Deposit Account Agreement," though Part VI is a part of that same Deposit Account Agreement, making the priority rule circular.
It gives Part VI priority over the rest of the instrument, while the introductory clause treats Parts I-VI as one Agreement and states no order of precedence.
"[Y]our primary deposit account" is undefined, and nothing in the Agreement says how a primary account is identified where a customer holds several.
It selects a different connecting factor from the Governing Law clause in Part I, which applies the law of the jurisdiction where the Store at which the Account was opened is located.
